lead: A system is an operator that turns an input signal into an output signal. Write it as y(t)=T{x(t)} in continuous time and y[n]=T{x[n]} in discrete time. The same idea covers an RC filter, a car suspension and a monthly savings balance. Engineers classify systems by memory, causality, stability, linearity, time invariance and invertibility because each label predicts how the system will behave in analysis and design. This chapter sets out those labels and shows how blocks connect in series and parallel.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for CT and DT signals, and Chapter 1.3 for the unit step used in the example.

sections.h3: A system maps input to output

blocks.text: A system is any rule, device or process that acts on an input signal and produces an output signal. Write the action as an operator T. For a continuous-time (CT) input x(t), the output is y(t)=T{x(t)}. For a discrete-time (DT) input x[n], the output is y[n]=T{x[n]}. Here t is real time in seconds; n is an integer sample index with no unit. The set of allowed inputs is the input set, and the set of resulting outputs is the output set.

The label CT or DT comes from the independent variable of the signals, not from the hardware. An RC low-pass circuit with voltage vᵢ(t) in and vₒ(t) out is CT. A car suspension with road height as input and body height as output is CT. The on/off command sequence for a room heater, recorded once per minute, is DT. A bank balance updated once per month, with balance B[n], deposits d[n] and interest rate r, is DT: B[n]=B[n−1]+d[n]+rB[n−1].

A computer can simulate a CT model by taking small time steps. The model is still CT because its signals are defined for every real t. This distinction matters when you sample a CT signal for processing; see Unit 5, Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems.

Large systems are built from smaller blocks. Two connections appear everywhere. In a series or cascade connection, the output of the first system feeds the second: y(t)=T₂{T₁{x(t)}}. In a parallel connection, the same input drives both blocks and the outputs add: y(t)=T₁{x(t)}+T₂{x(t)}.

The DT forms are identical with square brackets: y[n]=T₂{T₁{x[n]}} for series, and y[n]=T₁{x[n]}+T₂{x[n]} for parallel. The order matters in series. A filter followed by an amplifier is not the same as the amplifier followed by the filter when the amplifier clips.

An audio chain is a series connection: microphone, equaliser, amplifier, speaker. A stereo mix is a parallel connection: left and right channels add into a sum. In a control loop the blocks also connect in feedback, but that needs the transfer-function tools of Unit 4.

When blocks are linear and time-invariant, let h₁(t) and h₂(t) be their impulse responses. A series connection has overall impulse response h₁(t)*h₂(t), a convolution; in DT use h₁[n]*h₂[n]. A parallel connection has h₁(t)+h₂(t), or h₁[n]+h₂[n] in DT. In the Laplace domain these become the product H₁(s)H₂(s) and the sum H₁(s)+H₂(s); in the z domain use H₁(z)H₂(z) and H₁(z)+H₂(z). Unit 2 covers convolution.

sections.h3: Six labels used to classify systems

blocks.text: Classification answers practical questions before any calculation. The labels below are independent: a system can be, for example, causal and nonlinear.

items: Memoryless (static) or with memory (dynamic). A memoryless system uses only the present input. y(t)=3x(t)+2 is memoryless. A system with memory uses past or future inputs, or past outputs. y[n]=x[n]−x[n−1] has memory because it needs x[n−1].

Causal or noncausal. A causal system output at any time depends only on present and past inputs, never future inputs. y[n]=x[n]+x[n+1] is noncausal because it looks one step ahead. All real-time physical systems are causal; stored data can be processed noncausally.

Stable or unstable. A system is bounded-input bounded-output (BIBO) stable if every bounded input gives a bounded output. An audio amplifier with a fixed gain is stable; a microphone too close to its own speaker can become unstable.

Linear or nonlinear. A system is linear if it obeys superposition: T{a x₁+b x₂}=a T{x₁}+b T{x₂} for any inputs x₁ and x₂ and constants a and b. y(t)=3x(t)+2 is nonlinear because of the +2. y[n]=x[n]−x[n−1] is linear.

Time-invariant or time-varying. A time-invariant system does not change its rule with time: a shift in the input produces the same shift in the output. A resistor is time-invariant; a circuit switched on at t=0 may be time-varying during start-up.

Invertible or noninvertible. A system is invertible if different inputs always give different outputs, so an inverse system can recover the input. y(t)=3x(t) is invertible with inverse x(t)=y(t)/3. y[n]=x[n]² is not invertible over all real inputs because x and −x give the same output.

blocks.text: The formal tests for linearity, time invariance, causality and stability are in Chapter 1.6. Here the aim is the meaning, not the test routine. Some syllabi call this system classification and speak of a system as an interconnection of elements.

To classify a system from its equation, ask three questions in order. First, is the independent variable t or n? That fixes CT or DT. Second, does the output at an index use any other index? If yes, the system has memory; if no, it is memoryless. Third, does the output use a future index? If yes, it is noncausal.

items: Write the output for a general input, not for one numerical input.
List every input value that appears on the right-hand side.

If only plain x(t) or plain x[n] appears, the system is memoryless. Any argument other than plain t or plain n — a shift x(t−a), an advance x[n+k], or a scale x(2t), x[2n] — means the system has memory. Scaling or advancing the index also makes the system noncausal.
If x(t−a), x[n−k] or x[n+k] appears, it has memory; x[n+k] with k>0 also makes it noncausal.
Check any added constant or product of inputs: either can make the system nonlinear.

blocks.text: A CT model is used for a physical device described by differential equations. A DT model is used for software, sampled data and sequences. A single system, such as a digitally controlled motor, may need both: a CT model of the motor and a DT controller. Sampling links the two in Unit 5.

examples.question: A CT system is y(t)=3x(t)+2 and a DT system is y[n]=x[n]−x[n−1]. Classify each as CT or DT, and as memoryless or with memory. For x(t)=u(t), find y(1); for x[n]=n u[n], find y[2]. Justify each label in one line.
steps: Read the independent variable. The first system uses t, so it is CT. The second uses n, so it is DT.
Check memory. In y(t)=3x(t)+2 the output uses only x(t), so the CT system is memoryless. In y[n]=x[n]−x[n−1] the output uses x[n−1], so the DT system has memory.
For the CT input x(t)=u(t), at t=1 the unit step value is x(1)=u(1)=1 because 1 is positive.
For the DT input x[n]=n u[n], x[2]=2u[2]=2×1=2 and x[1]=1u[1]=1×1=1.
examples.answer: The CT system is memoryless with y(1)=5, and the DT system has memory with y[2]=1, in the units of the signals.
examples.check:
x1 = 1
y1 = 3*x1 + 2
x2 = 2
x0 = 1
y2 = x2 - x0
print(y1)
print(y2)

traps: CT and DT describe the independent variable. A digital computer that simulates a CT model does not make the model DT.
Causal is not the same as memoryless. y[n]=x[n−1] is causal but has memory; y[n]=x[n+1] is noncausal.
A constant term breaks linearity. y(t)=3x(t)+2 is nonlinear and time-invariant, not linear.
Stability and time invariance are independent. A system can be time-invariant and unstable, for example y[n]=2y[n−1]+x[n], an accumulator whose loop gain 2 makes the output grow without bound.
Squaring is not a small detail: y[n]=x[n]² is nonlinear over real inputs and not invertible, because x and −x give the same output.

quiz.q: Write the operator forms for a CT system and a DT system.
quiz.a: y(t)=T{x(t)} for CT; y[n]=T{x[n]} for DT; t is real time, n is an integer index.

quiz.q: Why does a numerical simulation not turn a CT model into a DT system?
quiz.a: The model's signals are still defined for every real t; the simulation only computes samples at small steps.

quiz.q: Is y(t)=x(t−1)+3 time-invariant? Give a one-line reason.
quiz.a: Yes. Shifting x by t₀ shifts y by t₀; the +3 is unchanged.
Every bounded input produces a bounded output.

quiz.q: Give one CT and one DT physical example.
quiz.a: An RC circuit is CT; a monthly bank balance is DT.

quiz.q: For y(t)=3x(t)+2 and x(t)=u(t), find y(−1).
Is y[n]=x[n]² over all real inputs invertible? Explain.
quiz.a: No. x[n]=2 and x[n]=−2 both give y[n]=4, so the input cannot be recovered.

beyond: Not for the exam. System classification feeds model-based design in control, communications and instrumentation. Digital twins keep a CT model of a plant beside a DT controller and update both from sensor data. In machine learning, a layer is a system with memory only through its stored state, so causality and stability become training constraints. Search for 'hybrid system', 'digital twin' and 'real-time simulation' to go further.
